en: Preface to the Text for Encouraging the Arousing of Bodhicitta, composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Guifeng at Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
To arouse bodhicitta is to venerate virtue, expand one’s deeds, empty the mind, and disregard the self; it is what is called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Unless one is...

Who else but one who has attained the vast and expansive Way, who possesses a nature of benevolence and forbearance, and who harbors far-reaching and great aspirations, could have conceived such an intention?

Indeed, it was during the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha-dharma had declined and people of the later age had little faith, that there appeared a superior scholar of the Confucian school, Lord Pei of Hedong, who embodied this benevolence. It was with him, Pei Gong, that I shared a friendship.

Having long known that he had entered the Buddha’s gate and reached the Buddha’s realm, and having read his essay on exhorting others to resolve upon Bodhicitta, I know him to be a messenger of the Buddha performing the Buddha’s work. As a son of the Buddha, how could I not be moved by this and leap for joy?

All who have taken refuge in the Buddha may treasure this as a mirror for self-reflection. Yet, the gateway to the Buddha-dharma is difficult to enter; failure therein lies in partiality and deviation.
The realm of the Buddha is difficult to reach; failure therein lies in negligence and haste. To seek the Dharma outside the mind, or to calculate a self within the body, is deviation.

To value only the principle of nature, or to rely solely on causes and conditions, is partiality. To cling to understanding while remaining confused in practice, or to sink into emptiness and dwell in quiescence, is negligence.

To exhaust the body and weary the spirit while seeking to force a realization is to act with haste. Now, that which Master Pei has attained, practiced, expounded, and exhorted is entirely different from this;
it is what is called thoroughly understanding one’s own mind, whose virtue is equal to that of a Buddha, and which is not sought outside the mind.

Thoroughly understanding that form and consciousness are empty like illusions and transformations, he does not harbor self-conceptions of "I. Suchness and original enlightenment—this is what he possesses.
The fundamental principle is not merely [the practice of] conditions; the Four Truths and the Six Perfections are what it propagates. It is not solely [a matter of] nature;
through ritual, offerings, praise, and mindfulness, one leads by example and exhorts others. It is not a matter of rapid action; merit, wisdom, compassion, and vows are its diligent pursuit.

It is not a state of stagnant dwelling; with harmony of breath and fitness of spirit, one responds to affairs according to conditions. It is not toil or hardship; one adjusts according to the times and acts without [exhaustion].

This is for the purpose of awaiting [the ultimate], not for seeking personal realization. Thus, being fully endowed with all virtues and free from all afflictions, how could this not be entering the Buddha’s gate and reaching the Buddha’s realm?
Having long shared in his aspiration and having read his writings, I found them insufficient to express my admiration through mere verse; therefore, I have hastily composed this preface.
Hereafter, those who wish to enter the Buddha’s gate and create the Buddha’s realm should believe, accept, and practice this accordingly.
A Text Universally Exhorting Monastics and Laypeople to Resolve upon Bodhicitta, Composed by Pei Xiu, Chancellor of the Tang Dynasty.
I universally announce to the great assembly: whether monastic or lay, if there are those capable of together resolving upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...

Regarding the "Vow of the Mind": I vow that in every birth, whether as a monastic or a layperson, I shall always share the same lineage, the same destination, the same aspirations, and the same pursuits with all others;
that we shall together exercise great compassion and cultivate great wisdom, mutually assisting one another until we reach Bodhi. I announce this universally to the great assembly:
if there are those among the monastics or the laity who can likewise resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I vow—
Life after life, they shall always share in pure karma; each leading their own retinue, they shall transform sentient beings.
Within the assembly at the Dragon Flower, they shall together receive the Buddha’s prediction, extensively cultivating great vows until they reach Bodhi.
First, the definition of the term *bodhi*:
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfect Universal Knowledge. "Awakening" (覺) means "ultimate" (*anuttara*). "Correct" (*samyak*) means knowing according to reality.

"Universal" (*saṃ*) refers to immeasurable wisdom; it is the correct awakening through the knowledge of both the ultimate and conventional truths. This is the most supreme and wondrous path realized by all Buddhas. It is the [path] of the multitude...

This is the wondrous source, the very root of what sentient beings are deluded by. Having admired the Tathāgata and forever sought to leave all sufferings behind, they lament that their own bodies have long lost the great benefit;
thus, with a resolute spirit, they strive to seek the Buddha-body—this is precisely the initial arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, the essence of the bodhicitta is explained.
Having already generated the great mind of bodhicitta, one must recognize the essence of that bodhicitta.

Now, if the essence of bodhicitta does not arise from the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), there is no way to reach enlightenment (*bodhi*). Therefore, it is necessary to discern it clearly; only then is it the correct cause for the practice of the Dharma.

Furthermore, O Great Assembly, from time immemorial you have always regarded that which is your body as being composed of the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind—a body that gathers and disperses in turn, belonging to the category of impermanent phenomena; it is not your true self.

From time immemorial, you have also regarded that which is your mind as being the deluded mind that perceives objects through conditions—a mind that arises and ceases momentarily, belonging to [the category of impermanence].
Impermanence is not my mind. That which I possess is the true body, perfect, empty, and quiescent; that which I possess is the true mind, vast and luminously aware.

(Perfect means that the infinite merits of the *dharmakāya* are inherently complete from the beginning. Empty and quiescent means that the *dharmakāya* is free from all phenomenal forms and is eternally unmoving.

Vast means that the essence of the true mind encompasses the *dharmadhātu* and contains empty space. Luminously aware means that it is clearly discerning and its reflection is pure and penetrating. This empty-quiescence and spiritual wisdom is divine...
Its function is sovereign; its nature contains myriad virtues, and its essence is free from a hundred negations.

It is like the pure lunar disk, perfect and without defect, yet when shrouded by the clouds of delusion, one does not realize it for oneself. Once delusive ignorance is removed, the true mind is fundamentally pure.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, all sentient beings, and this mind of mine—these three are without distinction. This is the very essence of the bodhicitta. To relinquish...

This is not what you acknowledge; instead, you acknowledge your own deluded thoughts, following death with rebirth and suffering alongside birds, beasts, and other miscellaneous species as their equals.

As a man of noble character (*puruṣa*), are you not ashamed? Having already resolved upon the mind of supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*), you ought to perform the deeds of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*):
give rise to the three minds, establish the five vows, cultivate all dharmas that assist toward bodhi, and take all Buddhas as your teachers.
Taking Bodhisattvas as companions, taking the sentient beings of the six realms as kinsmen, and taking the afflictions of birth and death as a garden—
vowing to rescue and deliver them until the end of the future— is what is called generating the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, the three minds are explained.

First is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Having realized that one’s own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, one consequently feels pity for those in the six realms who suffer in vain through their sinking and drifting.

Although one has not yet personally realized *bodhi*, one vows that sentient beings shall attain liberation (as the Sūtra says: "Although I have not yet crossed over myself, I vow to deliver those who have not yet crossed").

Laozi said: "The sage places himself last, and thus he is first. The Confucians say: "The benevolent person extensively bestows gifts and rescues the multitude; putting others first and oneself last. (Thus, all three teachings are the same.

Thereupon, one extensively manifests great compassion based on the realization of the same essence, and throughout the future, practices the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in those sentient beings, causing them all to return to the truth and together achieve the Buddha-way.
This is the mind of great compassion. Second is the mind of great wisdom. Having aroused great wisdom, one vows to deliver all classes of beings.

Since the categories [of sentient beings] are manifold and their faculties vary, one must extensively serve all Buddhas and widely study the wondrous Dharma, entering into realization one by one to transform sentient beings;
this is the mind of great wisdom (*mahājñāna-citta*). Third is the mind of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-citta*):

desiring to universally deliver sentient beings, one consequently gives rise to vast compassion and wisdom. However, although the mind is fundamentally pure, it has long been obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
It is difficult to suddenly eliminate [afflictions]. Those who are vessels for the Dharma must rely on the polishing of jewels.

Fearing that they might wander through the various realms of saṃsāra and fail to encounter the superior conditions of the Buddha-dharma, one gives rise to the great vow and fully cultivates the myriad practices. When practice and vow support one another, they are like the two wheels of a chariot;

moving forward without retreating, they lead directly to Bodhi. This is the mind of the great vow. (The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The lamp of the bodhicitta takes great compassion as its oil and the great vow as its wick.")
Great wisdom serves as its light). Nevertheless, among these three minds, the great vow is primary. One constantly maintains compassion and wisdom to deliver all sentient beings;
therefore, when first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one must first give rise to the vow. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s Chapter on Vows and Practices* states:
"When a person approaches the end of life, at the final moment, all their faculties completely disintegrate, and all kinsmen and relatives completely abandon them. One...
All power and majesty shall utterly perish; all wealth and treasures shall no longer follow one.
Only this King of Vows shall not abandon you, constantly acting as your guide until you reach Bodhi. Therefore, when you hear this King of Vows, do not give rise to doubt.
(This was spoken by Samantabhadra at the conclusion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; it is certainly not false. Practice according to this.)
Next, the five vows are explained:
first, the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings; second, the vow to accumulate boundless merit and wisdom;
third, the vow to study boundless Buddha-dharma; fourth, the vow to serve boundless Tathāgatas; fifth, the vow for the unsurpassed [enlightenment].
The vow for perfect enlightenment is fulfilled by maintaining these five vows, directing the mind in every thought-moment without interruption;
this constitutes possessing the great mind of bodhi and upholding the precepts of the bodhicitta. The three minds and five vows mutually support one another in layers;
the path of all Buddhas is identical and does not exceed this. This is precisely the full realization of the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers to uplifting the mind.

Next, one should exhort the constant maintenance of the bodhicitta by universally addressing the great assembly, whether monastics or laypeople: "Since you have already generated the great mind of bodhi and are practicing the wondrous path of the bodhisattvas..."

With utmost sincerity, I universally invoke all Buddhas; with single-minded devotion, I universally embrace all sentient beings. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, I shall constantly maintain this vow:
never to deceive those in the six realms, never to fail the Tathāgatas in my faith, and to extensively establish ferries and bridges to protect and uphold the teachings.
Beneath Maitreya’s seat, they have all realized non-arising; within the assemblies of the thousand Buddhas, they shall all serve as leaders.
If one can maintain this mind, then they will never again fall away from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Next, he exhorted the liberation of sentient beings by addressing the great assembly—both monastics and laypeople alike: "From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, I vow to deliver all sentient beings, universally causing them to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
For those on the dark shore, I shall act as a bright lamp; for those in the ocean of birth and death,"
It serves as a boat or raft. Although your strength may not yet suffice, you must constantly maintain this mind, continuing it from moment to moment without interruption.
Are you able to uphold this mind? If you uphold this mind, you will never again fall away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, he exhorted the accumulation of merit by addressing the great assembly—

both monastics and laypeople alike— vowing that from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, they would accumulate merit within the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) and the field of reverence (*guru-kṣetra*).
Furthermore, they were to relinquish both internal and external wealth to accomplish the foundation of the ten thousand practices for the sake of sentient beings.
The Way must be supported by the superior conditions of merit and virtue to eliminate self-centered thoughts and enable one to receive the retribution of gods and humans.
Although your strength may not yet suffice, you should constantly cultivate this mind, maintaining it in a continuous succession of moments without interruption. Are you able to maintain this mind?
If one maintains this mind, one will never fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Next,
he exhorted them to study and practice the Buddha-dharma,

universally addressing the great assembly— whether monastics or laypeople— vowing that from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, they would cultivate all the Buddhas' [teachings].

Regarding the Dharma: you have thoroughly mastered all gates of teaching—the four immeasurable minds, the six pāramitās, the depth and shallowness of the meaning of the teachings, the existence and non-existence of cause and effect, the two schools of nature and characteristics, and the two teachings of sudden and gradual. You have attained complete penetration in all these matters.

Although your power may not yet reach the point of opening the way for sentient beings, you constantly maintain this resolve, with each thought following the next in uninterrupted succession. Are you able to sustain this mind? If...
Maintaining this mind, one shall never again fall away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Next,

he exhorted those who were personally attending the Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to announce it universally to the great assembly— both monastics and laypeople— that from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, they vowed to serve all Buddhas.
All great Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends never tire of seeing spiritual friends; they never grow weary in mind of serving spiritual friends;
and hearing all the instructions of spiritual friends, they joyfully and happily practice them in accordance with them.

They constantly study the conduct practiced by the youth Sudhana; though their power has not yet reached that level, they always maintain this resolve, with every thought succeeding one another in continuity.
Do not allow it to be interrupted. Can you maintain this mind? If you maintain this mind, you will never fall back or lose *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, he exhorted them to practice with the sole aim of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood,
announcing to the great assembly— whether monastics or laypeople alike— that from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, they should always vow to become Buddhas in the future.
Do not give rise to the mind of the two vehicles. Vow that you and all sentient beings may be of one essence and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
Dedicate every single wholesome deed you cultivate toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As for the sentient beings whom you exhort...
I cause each and every one of you to resolve upon the unsurpassed path. Constantly cultivate the power of the vast compassionate vows of the Brahmā-śramaṇa Ratnasāgara.
Although you may not yet be able to perpetually maintain this mind in a continuous succession of moments without interruption, are you able to uphold it?
If you uphold this mind, you shall never again fall away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Next, he exhorted the assembly of monastics and laypeople to form a bond, announcing to the great multitude: "Whether monastic or lay, from this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, may you together with all monastics and laypeople who have likewise resolved upon bodhicitta, never be separated throughout birth after birth. May we share the same vows, the same mind, the same conduct, and the same virtue, each cultivating [the path]."

Through concentration and wisdom, you shall transform sentient beings. Whether acting as brothers or as teachers and elders, you shall mutually exhort one another to resolve for enlightenment and protect and uphold each other.
If one person loses the way, you shall together rescue and deliver them; if one person realizes the Path, you shall together take refuge with them.
Never wearying or becoming fatigued, never abandoning or separating from one another—can you maintain this mind? If you maintain this mind, you shall never fall back or lose it.
[He attains] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Next, he exhorts [them] to master the complete and sudden (yuan-dun) scriptures and announces them universally to the great assembly, whether monastic or lay; having already resolved upon the great mind of bodhi and set in motion the great practice of bodhi.

If one does not penetrate the essence of the bodhicitta and has not yet harmonized with the source of the bodhi-dharma, then even though one has already generated the aspiration for enlightenment, one will inevitably be hindered and crushed by the Lesser Vehicle.

Therefore, one must first realize that the perfectly luminous and pure awakening is fundamentally free of ignorance; that illusory cataracts and flowers in the sky are both devoid of substantial reality;
and that by remaining far removed from grasping and attachment, one becomes as level as space, constantly flowing forth from the heart of tranquil illumination the vast and great [Dharma].

Compassion and wisdom: in this way, one does not become mired in various marks nor fall into the two extremes; only then does one possess the true cause for Bodhi and avoid undergoing toil and suffering in vain.

Whether it be the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Awakening of Faith*, which are subtle, wondrous, penetrating, and luminous, or the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, which are vast and complete—if you share my aspiration, I hope that we shall both master these scriptures.

Next, it is explained how the Brahma-cārin Sarvabodhisattvadharmaratnasāgara exhorted immeasurable people to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereupon they all attained the prediction of their future Buddhahood.
He further exhorted three hundred million disciples to resolve their minds [upon enlightenment]; among them was one...
A man named Jyotiṣka addressed him, saying: "Venerable One, what is bodhi? What are the factors conducive to bodhi?
How does a bodhisattva practice for the sake of bodhi? How does one attain bodhi through the application of mindfulness? At that time, the teacher replied:
"Bodhi is precisely the four immeasurable treasuries cultivated and accumulated by a bodhisattva; that is to say, they are inexhaustible."

The treasury of merit, the treasury of inexhaustible wisdom, the treasury of inexhaustible insight, and the treasury of the harmonious integration of the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma—this is called bodhi.
As the Buddha has taught the factors that assist bodhi: namely, the dharma-gate of embracing purity and transcending birth and death.
Noble son, the relinquishing of wealth is a factor that assists bodhi; because it tames sentient beings, the observance of ethical discipline is a factor that assists [bodhi].
Because the qualities of awakening (*bodhidharma*) are accomplished according to one’s aspirations, patience (*kṣānti*) is an auxiliary to the qualities of awakening.
Because the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are fully perfected, diligence (*vīrya*) is an auxiliary to the qualities of awakening.

Because all matters are fully accomplished, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is an auxiliary to the qualities of awakening. Because the mind shall attain thorough subduing, wisdom (*prajñā*) [is an auxiliary to the qualities of awakening].
Wisdom is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it brings knowledge of all afflictions. Therefore, extensive learning is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it results in unimpeded eloquence.
Therefore, merit is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it provides for the needs of all sentient beings.

Therefore, reflection is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it accomplishes the severing of doubt. Therefore, a mind of loving-kindness is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it brings about [the perfection of...]

Because it is an unimpeded mind, the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) is an auxiliary dharma for awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Because it never tires of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the mind of joy (*muditā*) is an auxiliary dharma for awakening.
Because it engenders love and delight for the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is an auxiliary dharma for awakening.
Because it achieves the severance of attachment and aversion, listening to the Dharma is an auxiliary dharma for awakening. It achieves the cessation of the five [hindrances].

Because it transcends the world, renunciation is an aid to the factors of enlightenment. Because it abandons all worldly things, dwelling in solitude (araṇya) is an aid to the factors of enlightenment.
Because it extinguishes unwholesome karma, sympathetic joy is an aid to the factors of enlightenment. Because it increases roots of goodness, [it is likewise an aid].
Therefore, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), for they accomplish the discernment of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
Therefore, the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they involve the abandonment of all unwholesome states and the cultivation of all wholesome states.

Therefore, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they accomplish physical and mental lightness and agility (*praśrabdhi*). Therefore, the faculties (*indriya*) are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they [serve to] destroy...

Because it awakens one from all afflictions, awakening is a factor that assists enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Because it awakens to phenomena as they truly are, the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-samaya*) are factors that assist enlightenment.
Because it subdues sentient beings and causes them to become pure, this is called the "Dharma-gate of embracing purity and crossing over birth and death.
Practicing in this manner is precisely how one attains enlightenment through focused mindfulness. Such is the bodhicitta; now...
You should give rise to desire. This path is pure; this path is untainted; this path is upright; this path is secure.

You all should single-mindedly make great vows to take up the adornment of Buddha-lands according to your respective wishes (the adornments of the Buddha-lands are each different—some take pure lands, some take defiled lands; these are fully detailed in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*).
Next, the four factors of indolence for bodhisattvas are explained.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed Vipaśyanāmala, saying: "Bodhisattvas have four forms of indolence.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will undergo various sufferings within the prison of saṃsāra and will not be able to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Samyak-saṃbodhi. What are the four? They are: inferior conduct, inferior companions, inferior giving, and inferior vows. What is inferior conduct?
If there is a bodhisattva who violates the precepts of body and speech and does not skillfully guard their actions, this is called inferior conduct.
What is an inferior companion? To associate with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to engage in activities together with them—this is called an inferior companion.

What is inferior giving? It is when one is unable to relinquish all that one possesses, gives rise to discrimination toward the recipient, and practices giving for the sake of attaining heavenly pleasures; this is called inferior giving. What is an inferior vow?
It is when one is unable to single-mindedly vow to take up the pure and wondrous worlds of the Buddhas, and the vows one makes are unable to subdue sentient beings.
This is called the "Lower Vow" (from the *Cihua jing*).
Next, the four dharmas of the bodhisattva’s swiftness are explained;
there are further four dharmas which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, enable them to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
First, one is able to maintain the purity of the prohibitive precepts, practicing the dharma-gate of guarding and relinquishing through body, speech, and mind.
Second, one draws near to and studies under those who practice the Mahāyāna, engaging in activities together with them. Third, one is able to relinquish all possessions entirely.

To bestow [merit] upon all with a heart of great compassion; fourth, to single-mindedly vow to take up various adorned Buddha-worlds, also for the sake of taming all sentient beings. These are called the four dharmas (from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).
Next, the merit of generating the bodhicitta is explained.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "Son of the Buddha, what is the measure of the merit obtained when a bodhisattva first generates the bodhicitta?
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati replied: "This meaning is extremely profound; it is difficult to explain, difficult to know, and difficult [to fathom]."

It is difficult to discern; difficult to believe and understand; difficult to realize; difficult to practice; difficult to penetrate; difficult to contemplate; difficult to measure; and difficult to enter.
Nevertheless, O Son of the Buddha, I shall, by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, explain it for you.
Suppose, O Son of the Buddha, there were someone who provided all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings throughout incalculable worlds in the eastern direction, continuing for—
After one eon, he then instructs them to purely uphold the five precepts. It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Would the merit of this person be great? The Deva-Indra said, "The merit of this person can only be known by the Buddha.
Dharmamati said, "Compared to the merit of a Bodhisattva’s first resolve for enlightenment, [the former's merit] does not equal even a hundredth part."
And one part; a thousandth part does not equal it; a hundred-thousandth part does not equal it.

Likewise, a ten-millionth part, a hundred-billionth part, a trillionth part, a hundred-trillionth part, a nayuta-ten-millionth part, a hundred-nayuta-ten-millionth part, a thousand-nayuta-ten-millionth part, a hundred-thousand-nayuta-ten-millionth part, a million-nayuta-ten-millionth part, and so on...
It would not equal even one part in ten million billion *upaniṣad*s. Son of the Buddha, let this analogy suffice for now.
Suppose there were someone who, for a hundred kalpas, provided all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings throughout incalculable worlds in the ten directions;
and having done so, subsequently instructed them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action. Even with such offerings continued for a thousand kalpas, and the instruction...
They cause them to dwell in the four dhyānas for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; they cause them to dwell in the four immeasurable minds for billions of kalpas;
they cause them to dwell in the four formless absorptions for hundreds of billions of kalpas; they cause them to dwell in the fruit of srotāpanna for hundreds of billions of kalpas;

they cause them to dwell in the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin for trillions of kalpas; they cause them to dwell in the fruit of anāgāmin for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas; and for nayutas of kalpas...

If one were to instruct others for a hundred *koṭi* of eons to abide in the fruit of arhatship, and for a hundred thousand *nayuta-koṭi* of eons to instruct them in the path of a pratyekabuddha—would the merit of such a person be great? Śakra-devendra replied, "The merit of this person can only be known by a Buddha.
Dharmamati Bodhisattva said, "Compared to the merit of a bodhisattva’s first aspiration for enlightenment, the merit of this person is [insignificant]."
A hundredth part does not equal it; even a fraction as small as an *upaniṣad* does not equal it.

Why is this? When all Buddhas first resolve their minds on enlightenment, they do not merely intend to provide all manner of pleasant requisites for the sake of all sentient beings throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the ten directions for a period of a hundred *kalpas*, nor even for a hundred thousand *nayutas*.
Because of his immeasurable eons, he has resolved upon the bodhicitta not merely to instruct so many sentient beings to practice the five precepts and the path of ten wholesome actions,
nor to teach them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, nor to teach them to realize the fruit of srotāpanna,
sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or the path of the pratyekabuddha; rather, he has resolved upon the bodhi...
They focus their minds for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never interrupted; for the sake of pervading all worlds;
for the sake of delivering and liberating all sentient beings in all worlds; for the sake of fully knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds;
for the sake of fully knowing the defilement and purity of sentient beings within all worlds; and for the sake of fully knowing all worlds themselves.
Because their nature is pure; because they wish to fully know the mental inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
because they wish to fully know the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings; because they wish to fully know the faculties and skillful means of all sentient beings;
because they wish to fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings; because they wish to fully know the three [vehicles] of all sentient beings...
Because of worldly wisdom; because of the desire to fully know the equality of the spheres of all Buddhas;
and because of the arousal of the mind for unexcelled bodhi, one is constantly remembered by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
One shall receive the sublime Dharma from all Buddhas of the three periods of time and will immediately become equal in essence to all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Thus it is said.
One cultivates the methods for aiding the path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; one accomplishes the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
one adorns the unique Buddha-dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;

and one fully attains the wisdom of the Dharma-exposition of all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm. Why is this? Because by generating this resolve, one shall attain Buddhahood; thus it should be known.
This person is then equal to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they are equal to the realm of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they are equal to the merit of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. They attain the ultimate, equal, and true wisdom of the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies.
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, they are already [honored] by all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Praising them, they are immediately able to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings, subduing all beings throughout every world.
They are immediately able to cause all worlds to tremble; they are immediately able to illuminate all worlds;
they are immediately able to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms in all worlds; they are immediately able to adorn and purify all worlds; and they are immediately able, within all worlds...
Manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood within the realms, they are able to cause all sentient beings to attain a heart of joy;
they are able to enter the nature of all dharma-realms; they are able to uphold the lineage of all Buddhas; and they are able to obtain the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.
This bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind does not have even the slightest attainment regarding the three periods of time. If any...
The Buddha; or the qualities of the Buddhas; or the bodhisattvas; or the qualities of the bodhisattvas; or the pratyekabuddhas; or the qualities of the pratyekabuddhas;
or the śrāvakas; or the qualities of the śrāvakas; or that which is supramundane; or supramundane phenomena; or sentient beings.

If sentient beings seek only all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) with a mind free from attachment to any phenomena, this is called the merit of first generating the mind of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). (This is from the "Chapter on the Merit of Generating the Mind" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

This refers to the Bodhisattva at the first stage [bhūmi]. Here, it refers to the initial generation of the bodhicitta while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whereas its full accomplishment occurs upon reaching the first stage.)
Next, regarding the doubt concerning the distinction between ordinary beings and sages:
some may say that the great mind of bodhi is the realm of saints and sages, and is certainly not something that can be conceived or emulated by the shallow understanding of ordinary people.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva first abides in the [first] stage and gives rise to the great mind, they are immediately able to travel throughout the ten directions and extensively perform the works of a Buddha. Now...
"To exhort ordinary people with the Great Dharma—is this not because their faculties and capacities differ? He replied, "It is not so. Ordinary beings and sages share the same source;

fundamentally there is no distinction. It is only through a single moment of delusion that one brings about one's own sinking and drowning. If one awakens to the fact that the nature is inherently perfect and luminous,"
One then becomes equal to all Buddhas. By generating the bodhicitta within one's nature and practicing accordingly, one is a bodhisattva (a being of great mind).
Why suffer by disparaging oneself and claiming that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are excluded? Furthermore, while in the stage of an ordinary being, the three poisons are the root;
yet now, having vowed to renounce wealth and treasures to transform sentient beings, although one has not yet fully practiced, it is natural [that this occurs].
With little greed, they vow to practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to transform sentient beings; though they have not yet fully practiced them, their anger naturally diminishes.

With little anger, they vow to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to deliver sentient beings; though they have not yet fully realized them, their delusion naturally diminishes. When these three dharmas reside in the mind, one immediately becomes a vessel for the Dharma.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not sever afflictions (*kleśa*), but rather gives rise solely to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and majestic power. This gateway to the Dharma is indeed [profound].

This would be a hollow pretense; why then hesitate and not act? Furthermore, the resolve of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, whereas the resolve of one in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is the perfected bodhicitta.
If one were to wait until the first stage before arousing this mind, [it would be too late].
Before the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), what dharma should one practice? Apart from this correct path to enlightenment, everything else serves as a cause and condition for birth and death.
If one merely remains within saṃsāra, by what means could one realize entry [into the stages]?

Therefore, from the moment he first resolved his mind on enlightenment, Śākyamuni Tathāgata served immeasurable Buddhas throughout countless lifetimes; the bodhicitta he generated remained steadfast until he reached Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
It was only before the Buddha that he first received the distant prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). At the assembly of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he was first named Mahākaruṇā.
It required hundreds or thousands of lifetimes before he finally attained accomplishment. Therefore, I exhort all monastics and laypeople to emulate my original teacher, the World-Honored One.

Do not, upon merely discerning the gates of the teachings, claim to possess the profound Dharma-treasury; nor, upon having a rough understanding of the nature of the mind, assert with certainty that one must traverse the stages to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.
All sentient beings must seek all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have all planted roots of goodness;

their merit and wisdom are naturally vast and profound, and they shall forever serve as the leaders of the world’s path. I universally entreat the great assembly to show this text to this prefecture and other provinces.
Those who share a karmic affinity with me, upon seeing this text, should resolve to attain Bodhicitta. When wishing to resolve the mind, [one should...]

First, please relinquish material wealth according to your capacity. Either offer a single meal as an oblation to the Triple Gem, or paint a single image for a place of diligent practice (*sādhanā-maṇḍala*).

Thereafter, relying upon this primary text, reverently generate the Great Vow. (According to the *Sūtra of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa*, whenever each Buddha encountered a Buddha during their stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), they first made offerings to the World-Honored One with material treasures, even down to willow branches and pure water, and only then generated the Bodhicitta. According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, when the Brahmā-candidate Ratnākara exhorted immeasurable humans and devas to generate the Bodhicitta, he first had them...)
Offer these objects to the Buddha, and then make your vow. Since the Way of all Buddhas is the same, it is necessary to receive their guidance.
After this inspiration has been awakened, every thought that directs the mind becomes the true cause for attaining Buddhahood; you should therefore rejoice deeply within yourself.

The clergy and laity do not deviate from their fellow practitioners; how could mountains and rivers obstruct true wisdom? I am fortunate to have received this inscription of name and lineage from a traveler.
Recorded on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Kaicheng era by Pei Xiu, Prefect of Mianzhou.
Exhortation to Generate the Bodhicitta (End).
This *Bodhicitta-śāstra* was composed by Pei Xiu, the Chancellor of the Li Tang dynasty. It is truly the fundamental basis for our teaching for transforming the ordinary into the sacred.
Since the establishment of the printing blocks, it is imagined that many have drifted away from it; often, both monastics and laypeople have not [preserved it].

Extensively heard and seen, now sought from both ancient and modern sources and published for circulation, this serves as a modest response to the profound intent of kings and ministers who have protected and supported the Buddha Vehicle.
Written on the day of the full moon in the final month of summer in the *Ren-shen* year of the Xiang-sheng era, respectfully inscribed by Jingzhao.
On the eighteenth day of the fourth month in the third year of Kenpō, I obtained this manuscript from the Great Song Kingdom.

As I read it, my joy was even deeper. Consequently, on the night of the eighteenth day of the fifth month at the hour of the rat, I transcribed it word-for-word, adding the necessary phonetic kana characters, at the Rensei Sōan hermitage in Katsuragi.
May both clergy and laity rejoice in this shared endeavor. This was during a time belonging to the final age.
People lack the great resolve; now that they encounter this text, it is like finding a limitless mani-jewel in a defiled courtyard.
In the final age, there is reliance for attaining Buddhahood. May I require this text in every birth and lifetime. —Śramaṇa Gaobian.
